correctness.rationale: The support identity W=S/R is exact. For Gaussian edge differences, disjoint edges are independent, incident-edge absolute values have covariance kappa, and Cov(S,Q)=mu m while Var(Q)=2n. A bounded-degree dependency graph supplies O(n) connected r-tuples of summands; normalized cumulants vanish for all orders r>2 and the covariance matrix converges. The centered Gaussian radial expansion contributes the negative mu^2 alpha^2/2 correction. Cauchy-Schwarz in the vertex-degree sequence makes the limiting variance strictly positive. The exact spherical mean and boundary cases are consistent. Programmatic checks of 160 finite support identities and 3 Monte Carlo width variances passed, but these are only independent diagnostics, not proof by finite experiments.

originality.rationale: The claim is distributional and simultaneous over every bounded-maximum-degree connected graph sequence with converging edge and wedge densities. Exact first/second or even third width moments, tree extremizers, and deformation-cone descriptions do not imply its joint Gaussian/radial-normalization limit. The most directly relevant indexed prior claim is a finite-variance identity, compared by mathematical implication. Full text of one particularly close indexed record could not be read, and less-indexed Gaussian graph-variation CLTs could yield equivalent coverage; this PASS is a qualified comparison, not uniqueness certification.

value.rationale: This provides a natural full-distribution universality theorem for spherical widths of every bounded-degree connected graphical-zonotope graph sequence, with no limiting graph topology assumption beyond two local densities. It shows that asymptotic spherical width depends on edge and wedge densities alone although higher finite moments see other motifs, and identifies precisely the radial correction from intrinsic spherical normalization. Such a result distinguishes bounded-degree Gaussian behavior from growing-hub non-Gaussian phases and supports principled geometry of graphical arrangements. It is not merely a finite-moment computation or renaming of a normal-approximation theorem.
